summary: Describes an experiment in remote printing that uses ordinary Internet mail to carry a document to a printer connected to the telephone network, such as a fax machine. The idea is to let mail infrastructure do the long-distance delivery. It was replaced by RFC 1528, RFC 1529.

eli5.summary: Instead of driving a paper to a faraway office, you email it, and a machine near the other person prints it out for them.

questions: how to send mail to a fax machine
how to send fax over email
subtitle: Using Internet email to send print jobs to fax machines by telephone number.

tldr.problem: People who want to send printed materials to a remote location often do not have direct access to the recipient's printer. Fax machines exist at many locations, but there is no standard way to send them documents via email.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a special MIME content-type, application/remote-printing, that users can include in an email message along with the document to print. The recipient's printer is addressed using its telephone number, converted into a domain name and routed via email using standard DNS MX records.
tldr.outcome: An experimental implementation was launched in 1993, but it was superseded by more direct fax-to-email gateways defined in RFCs 1528 and 1529. The approach of routing printing through email did not become widely adopted.

facts.label: Phone number conversion
facts.value: Reversed and split into domain labels

today: RFC 1486 is Experimental and was superseded by RFC 1528 and RFC 1529. Email-to-fax services are now provided by dedicated gateway services rather than through the domain-based routing scheme proposed here.

sections.title: Remote Printing via Email
sections.content:
RFC 1486 describes an experiment in using the Internet email system to deliver documents to printers, including facsimile machines, at remote locations. Rather than developing a separate infrastructure or using a dedicated network service, the authors proposed using the email system's existing routing capabilities to carry print jobs to their destination.

The advantage of this approach is that it leverages the general-purpose email infrastructure already deployed worldwide. This allows any organization to make its printers accessible to the broader Internet community without requiring new network hardware or protocols. People could print to fax machines across the international telephone network simply by sending an email.
sections.eli5: The idea is to send a print job by email, just like sending a letter. The email system figures out where to send it based on the phone number of the printer, and then prints it out there.

sections.title: The Message Format
sections.content:
A remote printing email message contains two parts. The first part is a MIME content-type called application/remote-printing, which carries metadata about the recipient and originator: their names, organizations, contact information, and facsimile numbers. The second part is the actual document to print, which can be text, PostScript, a TIFF image, or other content types that have a natural printing representation.

The recipient address is constructed from the printer's telephone number by reversing the digits and treating each as a domain label under the special domain "tpc.int" (Telephone Publishing Community). For example, the phone number +1 415 968 2510 becomes the domain address "0.1.5.2.8.6.9.5.1.4.1.tpc.int", with the local part always "remote-printer". This address is then routed using standard email MX records, so that DNS wildcards can match ranges of phone numbers to the appropriate printer server.
sections.eli5: The email has two parts: first is information about who is sending it and who should get it (the cover sheet), second is the actual document. The phone number is written backwards as a fake email domain so the email system can find the right printer.

sections.title: The Experiment Infrastructure
sections.content:
The experiment used a distributed infrastructure organized around the special domain "tpc.int", divided into zones by IDDD country codes and area codes. Participating sites registered MX records that matched telephone number prefixes, allowing them to accept print jobs for printers within their service area. The North American zone for area code 415, for example, would have an MX record matching the pattern *.5.1.4.1.tpc.int.

A prototype implementation was made available in source form under Unix/SunOS, integrated with Sam Leffler's open-source FlexFAX package. The experiment included provisions for accounting, privacy (via minimal audit logs), and a mailing list for participants to coordinate. However, the RFC notes that the initial experiment did not address authentication, authorization, or advanced features like discovery of which content types a server could support.
sections.eli5: Different sites registered their phone number ranges with a central zone. When an email came in for a phone number, the system looked it up and sent it to the right printing server. A test program was available for people to try out.

sections.title: Status and Successors
sections.content:
RFC 1486 is marked Experimental and was superseded by RFC 1528 and RFC 1529, which defined alternative approaches to fax-over-email. The experiment in routing print jobs through the email infrastructure did not become widely deployed. Instead, the industry adopted dedicated fax servers and gateways that bridged fax and email more directly, rather than treating fax delivery as a special case of email routing.

The RFC remains a historical document showing one approach to integrating disparate communication systems through a general-purpose infrastructure. The addressing scheme and protocol design demonstrated creative thinking about leveraging existing systems, but the practical deployment challenges and the emergence of dedicated email-to-fax services made the approach obsolete.
sections.eli5: This was an experiment that didn't catch on. Within a year, better ways to send faxes through email were invented. The idea of using phone numbers as email addresses was clever but turned out not to be practical.
